promptText: In the tool-calling round trip, which statement best describes what the model actually does?
options: The model executes the tool's real code directly against your database or network
The model only produces a structured request naming a tool and arguments; your application executes the real code
The model and your application both execute the tool independently and compare results
The model delegates execution to the LLM provider's own infrastructure, bypassing your code entirely
explanation: The model never executes anything itself — it emits a structured 'call tool X with these arguments' proposal, and your application code is solely responsible for validating and executing the real method or service call.

promptText: Why must the real result of a tool execution be fed back into the conversation rather than the tool call itself being treated as the final answer?
options: Because providers require at least two API calls per conversation for billing purposes
Because the model's final answer must be grounded in what actually happened, not in what the model assumed would happen when it proposed the call
Because tool calls are always streamed and need a second request to complete the stream
Because Spring AI's ChatClient cannot render a tool-call object directly to the user
explanation: A tool call is only an intent/request; the model has no way of knowing the real outcome until your code executes it and the actual result is appended to the conversation for the model to reason over.

promptText: What is the primary purpose of the `description` attribute on Spring AI's `@Tool` annotation?
options: It is internal documentation only read by other developers maintaining the code
It is the primary signal the model uses to decide whether the tool is relevant and how to fill in its arguments
It configures the HTTP timeout for the tool's execution
It sets the JSON Schema 'title' field purely for cosmetic display in logs
explanation: The description is sent to the model as part of the tool spec and is the main input to the model's tool-selection and argument-filling decision — a vague description produces unreliable tool selection.

promptText: How do you register a `@Tool`-annotated bean so its methods are available to the model during a chat call in Spring AI?
options: Annotate the ChatClient class itself with @EnableTools
Pass the bean instance into `.tools(...)` on the ChatClient's fluent prompt call (or at builder configuration time)
Add the tool's fully qualified class name to application.yml under spring.ai.tools
Tools are auto-discovered from the entire classpath with no explicit registration needed
explanation: Spring AI reflects over objects passed to `.tools(...)` to discover `@Tool` methods and build `ToolCallback`s from them; nothing is auto-registered without being explicitly passed in.

promptText: What does the ReAct pattern (Thought/Action/Observation) rely on that native, schema-constrained tool calling was specifically invented to eliminate?
options: The use of any system prompt at all
Text parsing of an unstructured model completion to extract an action to execute
The requirement that models be fine-tuned before they can call tools
A dependency on vector databases for tool discovery
explanation: ReAct formalized alternating Thought/Action/Observation text, but your code still had to regex-parse the 'Action' line out of free text — native tool calling replaced this with a typed, provider-returned call object.

promptText: What happens by default in Spring AI when a `@Tool`-annotated method throws an exception during execution?
options: The entire chat request fails and an unhandled exception propagates to the caller
Spring AI silently retries the tool call up to three times before giving up
Spring AI catches the exception and converts it into an error result sent back to the model inside the ToolResponseMessage
The exception is logged but the model receives no message for that tool call at all
explanation: Rather than crashing the whole request, Spring AI's default behavior converts the exception into an error observation the model can reason about, so it can react sensibly rather than the app failing outright.

promptText: A `@Tool` method takes a raw `String query` argument that is concatenated directly into a database query inside the tool body. What is the most accurate characterization of the risk?
options: There is no real risk because JSON Schema validation already guarantees the string is safe
The risk is structurally identical to SQL injection, because the model's argument generation can be influenced by adversarial content from documents, tool results, or user messages
The risk only exists if the model is run at temperature above 0.7
The risk is eliminated automatically as long as @ToolParam(required = true) is set
explanation: Schema validation only guarantees shape (it's a string), not safety of content — a freeform argument used to build a query is exactly as vulnerable to injected/adversarial content as any other untrusted input, so parameterized queries and narrow structured parameters are required mitigations.

promptText: Why should the current user's identity be passed to a tool via Spring AI's `ToolContext` rather than as a model-supplied argument?
options: ToolContext is faster because it avoids JSON serialization entirely

A model-supplied argument is part of the schema the model (or injected/adversarial content) controls, so it could be forged; ToolContext lets the application inject the real authenticated identity outside the model's control
ToolContext is required because @Tool methods cannot accept String parameters
ToolContext automatically encrypts all arguments passed to the tool
explanation: Anything in the tool's JSON schema is something the model (or a prompt-injected instruction) can set to an attacker-chosen value; ToolContext is a side-channel the model never sees, letting your code supply the real authenticated caller's identity for authorization.

promptText: What does the `returnDirect = true` attribute on `@Tool` change about the tool-calling loop?
options: It forces the tool to execute asynchronously on a background thread
It skips the second model round trip and treats the tool's raw result as the final response of the interaction
It disables authorization checks for that specific tool
It causes the tool's JSON schema to be hidden from the model
explanation: returnDirect is appropriate when a tool already produces a complete, user-ready payload (like a generated chart or document link) — sending it back through the model a second time would add cost and latency, or risk the model paraphrasing structured data it shouldn't touch.

promptText: Two tools registered on the same ChatClient call happen to share the same name. What is the actual, documented consequence in Spring AI, as opposed to a common assumption?
options: Spring AI automatically namespaces them by owning class to avoid collision
The request fails fast at registration time with a clear naming-conflict exception
One callback silently overwrites the other in the internal name-keyed resolution map (last one wins) rather than a graceful merge
Both tools are merged into a single tool that accepts the union of their parameters
explanation: Because the provider and Spring AI both correlate a tool call to a definition purely by name, duplicate names result in silent overwrite rather than an error — which is why explicit, namespaced tool names are recommended over relying on Java method names.

promptText: By default, when the model requests two independent tool calls in the same turn, how does Spring AI's internal execution handle them?
options: It executes them concurrently on separate threads, so latency is roughly the slowest call
It rejects the second call and only executes the first one
It executes them sequentially on the calling thread, so total latency is the sum of both calls' execution times
It always defers the second call to the next conversation turn
explanation: Spring AI's default internal execution processes parallel tool calls one after another on the calling thread rather than fanning them out concurrently — a real latency cost for independent, slow tool calls unless execution is taken over manually to dispatch them concurrently.

promptText: What is the core difference between JSON-schema argument validation (enforced by the provider) and the semantic/business validation a tool implementation must still perform?
options: They are redundant — passing schema validation guarantees the request is also business-valid
Schema validation only guarantees shape (correct types, enum membership); it says nothing about ownership, state, or business invariants like whether an order actually exists or belongs to the caller
Semantic validation is only needed for tools marked returnDirect
Schema validation is optional and can be replaced entirely by Bean Validation annotations
explanation: A syntactically valid orderId that doesn't exist, belongs to another customer, or was already refunded passes schema validation cleanly — exactly the checks that prevent real harm require separate, explicit business validation inside the tool.

promptText: A support chatbot has a refund tool available. According to the chapter's security guidance, which combination of safeguards is described as necessary, rather than 'prompting the model carefully'?
options: A well-written tool description plus a low temperature setting to reduce over-eager calling

Authorization tied to the real authenticated user inside the tool implementation, amount/frequency caps, an explicit confirmation step, and audit logging — because probabilistic judgment is never an acceptable sole gate on an irreversible action
Registering the refund tool only when the user's message contains the word 'refund'
Disabling the refund tool entirely and requiring a human to trigger it via a separate admin panel with no model involvement
explanation: The chapter explicitly frames prompting as a probabilistic control that is insufficient alone for financial/destructive actions — real safeguards must sit in the trusted execution layer: authorization against the real caller, bounded blast radius, confirmation, and audit logging.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that registering many semantically overlapping tools measurably degrades reliability, and what follows from that mechanism?
options: Because Spring AI enforces a hard limit of 5 tools per request and silently drops extras

Tool selection is a probabilistic decision over a distribution of possible next outputs; overlapping descriptions flatten that distribution and increase wrong-tool-selection rates, so curation (narrow scope, precise/distinguishing descriptions, scoping the exposed subset) is the fix rather than better prompting
Because overlapping tools cause a JSON Schema naming collision that always throws an exception at startup
Because the model can only see the first three tools alphabetically in any given request
explanation: Tool selection is resolved the same way any next-token decision is — as a probability distribution; semantically similar descriptions increase ambiguity and wrong-tool selection, which is why the fix is precise, narrowly-scoped tool curation, not more prompting.

promptText: For a tool that must run arbitrary generated code (a 'code interpreter' style tool), what does the chapter identify as the only adequate control, as opposed to schema validation or prompt engineering?
options: Requiring @ToolParam(required = true) on every input to the code interpreter

Running the execution in an isolated, ephemeral sandbox (locked-down container/microVM, restricted filesystem, no or tightly scoped network egress) torn down after each call, entirely separate from the application process
Setting returnDirect = true so the model never sees the code's raw output
Increasing the temperature to 0 so the generated code is deterministic and therefore safe
explanation: The chapter is explicit that no amount of prompt engineering or schema constraint substitutes for a real security boundary — a powerful freeform capability like code execution needs infrastructure-level isolation, not application-level validation alone.
